summary: This RFC specifies interleaved modes for NTP. A packet's exact transmit time is known only after it is sent, so the modes let the timestamp be delivered in the next packet. This improves time synchronization accuracy in environments where the more accurate timestamps are available.

plainLanguage.summary: Mark exactly when you posted a letter on the next letter, since you only know the exact moment afterward. Clocks use that trick to get closer.

questions: how to improve ntp accuracy with transmit timestamps
how does ntp use transmit timestamps captured after sending
does ntp interleaved mode change the packet format
is ntp interleaved symmetric mode on by default
subtitle: NTP gets a trick for delivering a packet's true send time in the next packet, so clocks can be set more accurately.

tldr.problem: The best transmit timestamp for an NTP packet, captured in the driver or hardware, is known only after the packet has been sent, so it cannot be written into that packet.
tldr.mechanism: In the interleaved modes, each packet carries the transmit timestamp of the previous packet, and the origin timestamp acts as a cookie that tells the other side which earlier packet it refers to.
tldr.outcome: Clients and peers can compute offset and delay from more accurate transmit timestamps, while the packet header stays unchanged and the basic mode still works as a fallback. RFC 9769 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5905.

today: RFC 9769 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5905; no RFC obsoleting or updating it is recorded in the metadata for this site.

sections.title: Why Timestamps Arrive Late
sections.content:
Every NTPv4 packet carries four timestamps, two of which are the transmit and receive timestamps. For accurate synchronization they should be captured close to the start of the real transmission and the end of the real reception. The RFC lists four places to capture a timestamp: user space, the network device driver or kernel, the data link layer (MAC chip) and the physical layer (PHY chip). User-space timestamps are the least accurate; physical-layer hardware timestamps are the most accurate.

The catch is that a transmit timestamp captured in the driver or hardware is available to the NTP software only after it has sent the packet. It cannot go into that same packet unless the driver or hardware understands NTP and rewrites the packet on the way out. RFC 5905 has no way for a server to hand over such a later timestamp. A packet that strictly follows RFC 5905 is said to be in the basic mode.

Sending two packets per response would work, but the RFC rejects it: it would allow a traffic amplification attack, or use packets of unequal length, which would skew the network delay and the measured offset.
sections.plainLanguage: A clock helper learns exactly when it sent a message only after the message has left. The new modes let it tell you that time in its next message.

sections.title: Interleaved Client/Server Mode
sections.content:
The interleaved client/server mode differs from the basic one only in the values stored in the origin and transmit timestamp fields. The origin timestamp works as a cookie: it is a copy of one timestamp from the packet being answered, or zero if the packet is not a response. In the basic mode a request carries the transmit timestamp of the last valid response, and a response carries the transmit timestamp of the request. In the interleaved mode a request carries the receive timestamp of the last valid response, and a response carries the receive timestamp of the request. The transmit timestamp of an interleaved response belongs to the previous response that had that receive timestamp.

The server therefore has to remember pairs of local receive and transmit timestamps. It SHOULD discard old ones, for example with a fixed-length queue. It MAY separate them by IP address but SHOULD NOT separate them by port number, so that clients that change port between requests, as recommended in RFC 9109, still work. A server MUST NOT send a packet whose transmit timestamp equals its receive timestamp, so that interleaved packets can be told apart reliably; one way is to add 1 unit (about 1/4 of a nanosecond).

A server MUST NOT answer in the interleaved mode unless the request does not have equal receive and transmit timestamps and its origin timestamp matches a saved receive timestamp. Once used, that receive timestamp MUST NOT be used again. Otherwise the server answers in the basic mode. The first exchange is always basic, because the first request has a zero origin timestamp.

The protocol recovers from loss: if a request or response is lost, the client reuses the same origin timestamp, and the server answers in the interleaved mode if it still has the timestamps, or in the basic mode (saving new timestamps) if not. The client SHOULD limit how many interleaved requests it sends between server responses.

When a client gets an interleaved response it runs the RFC 5905 tests, with two changes. The duplicate check compares both receive and transmit timestamps, and the bogus check compares the origin timestamp with both the transmit and the receive timestamp of the request. Offset and delay are then computed with the RFC 5905 formulas using one of two sets of timestamps. The first set, RECOMMENDED for clients that filter on delay, uses the previous request and previous response; the second gives a more accurate current offset, but its delay is much more sensitive to frequency error between server and client because the interval between T1 and T4 is much longer.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side keeps a note of when it received things, and the next message points back to that note. The reply then tells the exact send time of the earlier message.

sections.title: Interleaved Symmetric Mode
sections.content:
The interleaved symmetric mode uses the same principles. A packet has a transmit timestamp for the previous packet sent to the peer and an origin timestamp equal to the receive timestamp of the last packet received from the peer. Both peers must support it for synchronization to work in both directions, so it SHOULD be disabled by default and turned on with an option on the active side of the association.

Peers do not always alternate their transmissions (for example when they use different polling intervals), so extra restrictions apply. Peer A MUST NOT send Peer B an interleaved packet unless all of the following hold: A has an active association with B configured for the interleaved mode, or has received at least one valid interleaved packet from B; A has not sent anything to B since it received the last valid packet from B; and A's previous packet to B was the only response to a packet from B. Without these rules a missing response could cause a mismatch that produces a large error in offset and delay.

A peer that has no association and answers with symmetric passive packets does not need to count packets, because each request has at most one response. It can work like a server in the interleaved client/server mode.
sections.plainLanguage: Two friends both write each other's earlier send times on their letters. They only do it when they have taken turns properly, so nobody mixes up which letter is which.

sections.title: Interleaved Broadcast Mode
sections.content:
An interleaved broadcast packet holds two transmit timestamps. One, for the packet itself, is in the transmit timestamp field. The other, for the previous packet, is in the origin timestamp field. This stays compatible with the basic mode, which uses a zero origin timestamp, and a client that does not support the interleaved mode simply ignores the origin timestamp.

A supporting client MUST check whether the origin timestamp is non-zero to detect an interleaved packet. It SHOULD also compare the origin timestamp with the transmit timestamp of the previous packet to detect lost packets; if the difference exceeds a maximum (the RFC gives 1 second as an example), the packet SHOULD NOT be used in the interleaved mode. If the client needs to measure network delay, it SHOULD use the interleaved client/server mode.
sections.plainLanguage: A town clock rings and announces the exact time of its previous ring. Anyone listening can use that to correct their watch.

sections.title: Impact of Implementation Errors
sections.content:
The interleaved modes make NTP more complex and more sensitive to implementation mistakes. The RFC looks at the likeliest errors in client/server mode. A client that does not support the mode but sets its origin timestamp to some other value can accidentally match a saved receive timestamp and trigger an interleaved response. It is expected to drop that response as bogus. If it did not check for bogus responses, it would get a corrupted measurement and be open to off-path attacks.

Even a client that accidentally implements the mode but rejects interleaved responses can still synchronize. Servers must not answer the same origin timestamp twice in the interleaved mode, so at least every other response is in the basic mode and accepted.

On the server side, receive and transmit timestamps that are not unique over a long enough interval can make a server wrongly answer a basic request in the interleaved mode, and the client drops it as bogus. A duplicated receive timestamp can make a response carry the transmit timestamp of a different response, which adds only a small error comparable to the error a basic response normally has.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone follows the rules slightly wrong, a message may be thrown away or a little off. The worst case is that you use the plain old way for that round.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security issues of the basic modes also apply to the interleaved modes; the RFC points to RFC 7384 for time protocols in general and RFC 5905 for NTP. Clients and peers SHOULD NOT leak the receive timestamp in packets to other peers or clients (for example as a reference timestamp), since an off-path attacker could use it as the origin timestamp for a forged interleaved response. Clients SHOULD randomize all bits of the receive and transmit timestamps in their requests to make the origin timestamp harder to guess.

Unlike in the basic mode, an interleaved client cannot set the origin timestamp to zero on every request to make tracking across networks harder. Attackers can also force a server to drop its saved timestamps, by flooding it, spoofing source addresses or replaying an authenticated request, so clients MUST NOT rely on servers being able to respond in the interleaved mode. Protecting symmetric associations against replay is harder than in the basic mode, because two consecutive valid responses are needed to complete a measurement.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the secret number on a message is a kind of password, you should not blab it to others. Keep a plain fallback ready in case someone interferes.
